#!/bin/bash
#flux: --job-name=respties
#flux: --output=std.%J.o
#flux: --error=std.%J.e
#flux: --nodes=2
#flux: --tasks-per-node=64
#flux: --exclusive
#flux: --time=1:00
# The LSF queue directive '-q compbiomed' has no direct Flux equivalent.
# This is typically handled by resource constraints or queue policies on the target system.

# go to the right directionary
cd $HCBASE/resp/tyk2_l5_l16

source /etc/profile.d/modules.sh
module load namd-gcc/2.12
#module load namd/2.13


NP=64
BASE_DIR=`pwd`

function schedule_system() {
    local lambda=$1
	local replica=$2

	echo "Scheduling ligand and complex for lambda $lambda replica $replica"
	LIG_PATH="lig/lambda_$lambda/rep$replica"
	COMPLEX_PATH="complex/lambda_$lambda/rep$replica"
    local LIG_TIMEOUT=$(( 60 * 60 * 4 ))

    # move to the correct ligand directory
    cd $BASE_DIR
    cd $LIG_PATH
	( 
        ( # then the complex part, no timeout
        cd $BASE_DIR && cd $COMPLEX_PATH &&
        # The 'mpiexec' command has been replaced with 'flux run'.
        # It will use the 64 tasks allocated to the sub-job.
        flux run -n $NP namd2    min.namd > min.log &&
        flux run -n $NP namd2    eq_step1.namd > eq_step1.log &&
        flux run -n $NP namd2    eq_step2.namd > eq_step2.log &&
        flux run -n $NP namd2    eq_step3.namd > eq_step3.log &&
        flux run -n $NP namd2    eq_step4.namd > eq_step4.log &&
        flux run -n $NP namd2    prod.namd > prod.log &&
        echo "Finished complex: lambda $lambda replica $replica"
        )
    ) &
}

#declare -a lambdas=(0.00 0.05 0.10 0.20 0.30 0.40 0.50 0.60 0.70 0.80 0.90 0.95 1.00)
#declare -a replicas=(1 2 3 4 5)

declare -a lambdas=(0.60)
declare -a replicas=(1 2)

for lambda in "${lambdas[@]}"; do
    for replica in "${replicas[@]}"; do
       # WARNING: This script launches independent NAMD simulations in the background.
       # The original LSF job requests 2 nodes with 64 tasks each. Each 'schedule_system' call
       # then launches a 64-task NAMD job. This means two simulations can run concurrently,
       # one on each node. Flux does not support submitting sub-jobs within a batch script in this manner.
       # This translation simply runs all simulations sequentially in the background on the first node.
       # This fails to replicate the parallelism of the original script.
       schedule_system $lambda $replica
    done
done

wait

However, all the `flux run -n 64` commands will contend for the same 64 cores on the first node, and the second allocated node will remain completely idle. This fails to replicate the parallelism of the original script and will likely lead to severe performance degradation due to oversubscription on the first node.
The script relies on an environment variable `$HCBASE` which is not defined within the script itself. The job will fail if this variable is not set in the environment from which the job is submitted.

issues: The script's execution logic is complex and potentially flawed. It launches two 64-task simulations as background processes. While Flux will correctly place one 64-task simulation on each of the two 64-core nodes, the `schedule_system` function itself runs sequentially. This means the second simulation (`lambda=0.60`, `replica=2`) will not be launched until after the first one (`lambda=0.60`, `replica=1`) has already started. More critically, each `flux run` command within the function is run sequentially (due to `&&`). The entire simulation for one replica (min, eq1, eq2, eq3, eq4, prod) must complete before the next `flux run` starts. A better approach for parallel execution would be to launch the two `schedule_system` calls in the background from the main script body.
The script relies on an environment variable `$HCBASE` which is not defined within the script itself. The job will fail if this variable is not set in the environment from which the job is submitted.
